subject: ELA
overview: English 9 runs about an hour a day: read the assigned text (aloud together when possible), discuss with text-dependent questions, then write. Read each text yourself before the week begins, require evidence (quotations with page or line numbers) for every claim, and use the paragraph and essay rubrics consistently so your child sees growth. Several texts include mature content (violence, racism, suicide in Romeo and Juliet); preview and discuss.

weeks.prep: Print or download "The Most Dangerous Game" (Project Gutenberg/CommonLit). Read it yourself first (about 30 minutes). Set up a notebook with tabs: Vocabulary, Quotes, Quick-writes. Note: the story involves hunting humans and some violence — fine for most 9th graders.
misconceptions: Calling every problem 'man vs. man': the story has several conflicts — Rainsford vs. Zaroff (person vs. person), vs. the jungle and sea (person vs. nature), and his own fear (person vs. self).
Treating the plot diagram's climax as 'the most exciting part' anywhere: the climax is the turning point where the main conflict is decided (the final confrontation in Zaroff's bedroom).
Summarizing instead of explaining quotations: after each quote, ask 'what does this show and why does it matter?'

days.guide: Explain how the reader's notebook will be used all year. Share a book that shaped you to model the reading autobiography, then have your child write one page about three books. Check that each book gets a 'why it mattered' sentence.

questions.q: What three sections will your reader's notebook have, and what goes in each?
questions.a: Vocabulary (new words with definitions and sentences), Quotes (memorable lines with page numbers and a note), Quick-writes (short timed responses).

days.guide: Draw the plot diagram (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution) and name the four conflict types. Read the first half together or independently; your child highlights suspense moments (e.g., the gunshots heard at night, the name Ship-Trap Island) and explains one.

questions.q: Early on, Rainsford says the world is made up of 'the hunters and the huntables.' Why is this ironic later?
questions.a: Rainsford, who doesn't care about the jaguar's feelings, becomes the 'huntable' — hunted by Zaroff — and learns what the prey feels.

questions.q: What type of conflict is introduced when Rainsford falls off the yacht?
questions.a: Person vs. nature (he must survive the sea and reach the island).

days.guide: Your child finishes the story and records three quotations showing Rainsford's attitude toward hunting, with two sentences of explanation each. Discuss whether his attitude really changes by the end.

questions.q: How do Rainsford's views of hunting change during the story?
questions.a: At first he dismisses the feelings of hunted animals; after being hunted himself he understands fear — he even says he now knows how an animal feels, though the ending (sleeping in Zaroff's bed) leaves his change ambiguous.

questions.q: What is the final line, and what does it suggest?
questions.a: 'He had never slept in a better bed, Rainsford decided.' It implies he defeated (killed) Zaroff without describing it.

days.guide: Make a three-column chart: foreshadowing, setting, pacing. Model one entry (the island's name and sailors' superstition foreshadow danger). Your child completes the chart and writes a paragraph arguing which technique creates the most tension.

questions.q: How does the name 'Ship-Trap Island' create suspense?
questions.a: It foreshadows danger — sailors fear it — so readers expect something sinister before Rainsford arrives.

questions.q: How does Connell's pacing change during the three-day hunt?
questions.a: Short sentences and quick action speed the pace and raise tension.

days.guide: Your child completes the plot diagram and the quiz (key). Then discuss: Is Rainsford a hero? Push for evidence on both sides.

questions.q: What is the climax of the story?
questions.a: Rainsford's surprise appearance in Zaroff's bedroom and their final confrontation, which decides the conflict.

weeks.assessment_key: Plot diagram: exposition — Rainsford and Whitney on the yacht discuss hunting and Ship-Trap Island; rising action — Rainsford falls overboard, reaches the island, meets Zaroff and Ivan, learns Zaroff hunts men, the hunt begins and Rainsford sets traps (Malay man-catcher, Burmese tiger pit, Uganda knife trap) and leaps into the sea; climax — he confronts Zaroff in the bedroom; resolution — 'He had never slept in a better bed.' Quiz answers (sample): 1) Ship-Trap Island. 2) General Zaroff. 3) Ivan, Zaroff's servant. 4) Zaroff got bored hunting animals because they cannot reason. 5) Rainsford refuses to hunt and is forced to be the prey. 6) He gets a three-day head start. 7) He creates traps from his hunting knowledge. 8) He jumps into the sea. 9) He hides in Zaroff's bedroom. 10) Implied: Rainsford kills Zaroff. 80%+ = proficient. Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence.

weeks.prep: Print "The Cask of Amontillado" (Project Gutenberg). Read it first; look up 'catacombs', 'nitre', 'motley', 'trowel'. Prepare a phrases reference sheet (prepositional, appositive, participial).
misconceptions: Taking Montresor at his word: he never names a single specific injury, so readers should question his reliability.
Mixing up verbal and dramatic irony: verbal = a character says the opposite of what he means; dramatic = the reader knows something a character doesn't.
Thinking every -ing word starts a participial phrase: in 'He was walking,' walking is a verb; a participial phrase acts as an adjective ('Walking deeper, Fortunato coughed').

days.guide: Read the story aloud together (about 20 minutes). Your child lists every claim Montresor makes about Fortunato and the 'thousand injuries,' then decides whether he is reliable.

questions.q: Does Montresor ever tell us what Fortunato's 'insult' was?
questions.a: No. He mentions a 'thousand injuries' and an insult but never gives specifics, which makes him an unreliable narrator.

questions.q: Who is the narrator and what point of view is used?
questions.a: Montresor, in first person, telling the story 'half of a century' later.

days.guide: Define verbal, situational, and dramatic irony. Model one example, then your child completes a five-example chart with effects.

questions.q: What is ironic about Montresor showing a trowel when Fortunato asks if he is a mason?
questions.a: Fortunato means the secret society (Freemasons); Montresor means a literal mason — he will use the trowel to wall Fortunato in. Dramatic/verbal irony.

questions.q: Why is 'I drink to your long life' ironic?
questions.a: Montresor plans to kill Fortunato that night — verbal irony.

days.guide: Highlight dread-building words in the catacombs (damp, nitre, bones, darkness). Your child rewrites one paragraph in a cheerful tone and notes what changed.

questions.q: Name three words or images in the catacomb scenes that create dread.
questions.a: Examples: piles of human bones, damp nitre 'hanging like moss', flambeaux that barely glow, the 'foulness of the air', the recess walled with stones.

days.guide: Teach prepositional (in the vault), appositive (Fortunato, a wine expert,) and participial (Laughing loudly, Fortunato...) phrases. Your child combines 10 sentences from their notebook and labels phrase types.

questions.q: Identify the phrase type: 'Fortunato, a proud man, followed Montresor into the vaults.'
questions.a: 'a proud man' — appositive phrase; 'into the vaults' — prepositional phrase.

days.guide: Timed paragraph (25 minutes), then the phrases mini-quiz. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: What are Fortunato's last words, and how does Montresor answer?
questions.a: 'For the love of God, Montresor!' Montresor replies, 'Yes, for the love of God!' — mocking his plea.

weeks.assessment_key: Timed paragraph proficient answer: claims Poe makes the revenge chilling through Montresor's calm, unreliable narration and irony; cites e.g. 'I drink to your long life' and 'Yes, for the love of God!' or 'My heart grew sick — on account of the dampness of the catacombs'; explains how his cold control and lack of remorse after fifty years ('In pace requiescat!') horrify the reader. Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence. Phrase quiz sample: 1) 'beneath the palazzo' — prepositional. 2) 'my friend' (in 'Fortunato, my friend,') — appositive. 3) 'Coughing violently' — participial. 4) 'during the carnival season' — prepositional. 5) 'wearing a jester's cap' — participial.

weeks.prep: Print "The Gift of the Magi". Gather two short mentor narratives (a memoir excerpt from CommonLit works). Prepare a clause reference sheet.
misconceptions: Calling the ending a 'twist' without explaining the irony: the gifts are now useless, yet the sacrifice proves their love — the irony carries the theme.
Choosing a narrative topic that is a whole summer or a list of events: a strong narrative zooms in on one turning point.
Confusing phrases with clauses: a clause has a subject and a verb; a phrase does not.

days.guide: Read the story together. Your child explains the situational irony and what O. Henry suggests about love and sacrifice, citing the closing comparison to the Magi.

questions.q: What does Della sell and what does she buy? What does Jim sell and buy?
questions.a: Della sells her hair (for $20) to buy a platinum fob chain for Jim's watch; Jim sells his watch to buy combs for Della's hair.

questions.q: Why does the narrator call them 'the wisest' givers?
questions.a: Because they sacrificed their greatest treasures for each other; their love, not the gifts, is the true gift.

days.guide: Point out the narrator's asides (e.g., the opening counting of $1.87, commentary on the Magi) and dialogue. Your child imitates one technique in a 150-word scene from life.

questions.q: How much money does Della have at the start and why repeat it?
questions.a: One dollar and eighty-seven cents; repeating it stresses her poverty and desperation.

days.guide: Your child maps 8 memorable moments, chooses a turning point, and drafts a story arc: setup, conflict, climax, reflection. Ask 'What changed in you?' to test the choice.

questions.q: What makes a moment a good 'turning point' for a personal narrative?
questions.a: It has a conflict and leads to a change in the writer — a new understanding, decision, or feeling that can be reflected on.

days.guide: Teach independent vs. dependent clauses and noun, adjective, and adverb clause types with examples. Your child writes 8 sentences about their memory using each type.

questions.q: Identify the clause type: 'The day that I broke my arm changed my summer.'
questions.a: 'that I broke my arm' — adjective clause (modifies 'day').

days.guide: Conference: your child presents their plan; you ask about the conflict and the reflection. They revise. Give the clause quiz.

questions.q: Identify: 'Because the bus was late, we missed the game.'
questions.a: 'Because the bus was late' — dependent adverb clause; 'we missed the game' — independent clause.

weeks.assessment_key: Conference checklist (each yes/no): a single focused turning point; a clear conflict; a planned climax; a planned reflection about change; an opening image or line chosen; revision made from feedback. Clause quiz answers (sample): 1) 'what she said' in 'I believed what she said' — noun clause. 2) 'who lives next door' — adjective clause. 3) 'when the storm hit' — adverb clause. 4) 'The lights flickered' — independent clause. 5) 'although I was nervous' — dependent adverb clause. 80%+ proficient.

weeks.prep: Have the narrative plan, a laptop or notebook, and a revision checklist (show-don't-tell, varied openings, dialogue punctuation, commas after introductory elements, consistent tense). Prepare the Unit 1 test.
misconceptions: Ending with a moral tacked on ('And that's why you should never give up'): reflection should grow from the story and show specific change.
Dialogue punctuation errors: punctuation goes inside the quotation marks, and a new speaker starts a new paragraph.
Shifting verb tense mid-story: pick past or present and keep it.

days.guide: Read two strong openings that start in action. Your child drafts the first half beginning with dialogue or a vivid image.

questions.q: Rewrite 'I was nervous before the race' as a showing opening.
questions.a: Sample: 'My shoelace had come untied three times, and each time my fingers shook harder.'

days.guide: Your child finishes the draft (800–1,200 words) through the climax and a reflective ending.

questions.q: What should a reflective ending do?
questions.a: Explain what the writer learned or how they changed because of the event, connected to specific moments.

days.guide: Highlight 'telling' sentences together; your child rewrites five as showing details and varies sentence openings with phrases and clauses.

questions.q: Revise 'She was angry' to show instead of tell.
questions.a: Sample: 'She slammed the cabinet so hard the plates rattled.'

days.guide: Edit with the checklist; type the final copy.

questions.q: Punctuate: I can't believe it she said
questions.a: "I can't believe it," she said.

days.guide: Your child reads the narrative aloud to family; then give the Unit 1 test.

questions.q: Name the four types of conflict.
questions.a: Person vs. person, person vs. nature, person vs. society, person vs. self.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric (W.9-10.3): 4 = engaging opening, clear sequence building to a climax, vivid sensory details and dialogue, varied sentences, meaningful reflection, nearly error-free; 3 = clear story and reflection, some telling, minor errors; 2 = list-like events, little detail or reflection; 1 = incomplete. Unit 1 test sample answers: 1) Climax of 'The Most Dangerous Game' — Rainsford confronts Zaroff in the bedroom. 2) Montresor is unreliable because he never specifies the insult. 3) 'I drink to your long life' — verbal irony. 4) Gift of the Magi ending — situational irony. 5) First-person point of view = narrator uses 'I'. 6) Identify a participial phrase and an adjective clause in given sentences. 7) Explain how foreshadowing builds suspense with one example.

weeks.prep: Print "The Necklace" (translation). Read it first. Prepare 8 sentences for semicolon practice.
misconceptions: Stating a theme as one word ('pride'): a theme is a full statement, e.g., 'Valuing appearances over honesty can cost a person everything.'
Putting opinions in an objective summary ('Mathilde was selfish'): stick to events.
Using a semicolon before a dependent clause or a list introduction: a semicolon joins two independent clauses.

days.guide: Read through the ball. Your child lists Mathilde's desires and the details that show her dissatisfaction.

questions.q: What is Mathilde unhappy about at the start?
questions.a: She feels she was born for luxury but married a minor clerk; she dreams of fine furniture, dresses, and jewels and is unhappy with her plain home.

days.guide: Finish the story; your child writes a 6-sentence objective summary.

questions.q: What happens after the ball?
questions.a: Mathilde loses the borrowed necklace; she and her husband replace it with one costing 36,000 francs, spend ten years in poverty repaying the debt, and then learn the original was fake (worth at most 500 francs).

days.guide: Model turning a topic into a theme statement; your child writes several, chooses the strongest, and supports it with three quotations.

questions.q: Turn the topic 'appearances' into a theme statement for the story.
questions.a: Sample: 'When people value how they appear to others over honesty, they may suffer far more than the truth would have cost.'

days.guide: Discuss 19th-century French class expectations (rank shown by dress and possessions). Teach semicolons joining related independent clauses; your child writes 8.

questions.q: Why didn't Mathilde simply tell Madame Forestier she lost the necklace?
questions.a: Pride and fear of shame — admitting it would hurt her reputation and status.

questions.q: Punctuate: Mathilde borrowed the necklace she lost it at the ball
questions.a: Mathilde borrowed the necklace; she lost it at the ball.

days.guide: Theme paragraph and quiz.

questions.q: What is the final ironic revelation?
questions.a: Madame Forestier's necklace was imitation (paste), so their ten years of hardship were unnecessary.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme paragraph proficient: a full theme statement (e.g., pride and concern for appearances lead to ruin) supported by two quotations (her dissatisfaction at the start; the years of labor; the final reveal) with commentary. Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence. Quiz answers: 1) Mathilde's husband is a clerk in the Ministry of Education/Public Instruction. 2) He gets an invitation to a ball. 3) She borrows a diamond necklace from Madame Forestier. 4) Replacement cost: 36,000 francs. 5) Ten years. 6) The necklace was fake. 7) Correct semicolon use in two sentences.

weeks.prep: Print "The Monkey's Paw" and "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge." Read both first. Parental note: Owl Creek opens with a Civil War hanging; The Monkey's Paw includes a grisly off-page death. Prepare colon examples.
misconceptions: Reading Part III of 'Owl Creek' as a real escape: the ending reveals the escape was imagined in the moments before Farquhar's death.
Assuming the paw's wishes are 'coincidences' or 'magic' without considering ambiguity: Jacobs keeps both explanations possible.
Colon misuse after a verb ('My favorites are: ...'): use a colon after a complete independent clause.

days.guide: Read 'The Monkey's Paw'. Your child keeps a foreshadowing log and predicts before each wish.

questions.q: What warnings does Sergeant-Major Morris give about the paw?
questions.a: He says a fakir put a spell on it to show that fate rules people's lives and those who interfere suffer; he throws it in the fire and says the first owner's third wish was for death.

questions.q: What happens after the first wish for £200?
questions.a: Herbert is killed in the machinery at work, and the company pays exactly £200 in compensation.

days.guide: Diagram the three scenes. Discuss why the final knock is never answered on the page.

questions.q: Why doesn't Jacobs show what is behind the door?
questions.a: Leaving it unseen lets the reader imagine something horrible and keeps the story ambiguous — the horror is stronger unseen, and Mr. White's third wish (that it go away) leaves only an empty road.

days.guide: Read 'Owl Creek'. Your child makes a timeline separating real time (seconds) from imagined time in Part III.

questions.q: What is the real event of the story?
questions.a: Peyton Farquhar, a Southern planter, is hanged from Owl Creek Bridge; his long escape in Part III happens in his mind in the instant before his neck breaks.

questions.q: What does Part II reveal?
questions.a: A flashback: a Federal scout disguised as a Confederate soldier tricked Farquhar into trying to burn the bridge.

days.guide: Your child writes a comparison paragraph on structure and surprise; teach colons introducing lists and explanations.

questions.q: How does Bierce's structure create surprise?
questions.a: He moves from the hanging (I) to a flashback (II) and then a detailed escape (III) told as real, so the final sentence revealing Farquhar is dead shocks the reader.

days.guide: Structure quiz; peer review with the rubric.

questions.q: Where is 'The Monkey's Paw' first wish made, in which part?
questions.a: Part I ends with the wish; the consequence arrives in Part II.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraph: Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence. Proficient content: Jacobs uses three scenes that each build to a wish and its consequence, withholding the final horror; Bierce uses nonlinear order and an imagined escape revealed only in the last line. Structure quiz answers: 1) Monkey's Paw has 3 parts. 2) Owl Creek's Part II is a flashback. 3) Farquhar imagines escape. 4) The last line reveals he was hanged. 5) Foreshadowing example: Morris's warnings. 6) A colon used correctly before a list.

weeks.prep: Obtain "Harrison Bergeron" (Vonnegut, in the anthology Welcome to the Monkey House or online at a library) and print "The Story of an Hour." Read both. Parental note: Harrison Bergeron has a shooting at the end.
misconceptions: Concluding Vonnegut is against equality: the satire targets forced sameness that drags everyone down, not equal rights.
Missing the irony of 'the joy that kills': the doctors think she died of joy at seeing her husband; readers know it was the shock of losing her new freedom.
Writing a thesis that is a fact ('Mathilde loses a necklace'): a thesis must be arguable.

days.guide: Read 'Harrison Bergeron'. Your child lists each handicap and the idea it exaggerates.

questions.q: What handicaps do George and the ballerinas wear?
questions.a: George wears a mental-handicap radio that blasts noises to stop his thoughts and a bag of birdshot weights; the ballerinas wear weights and masks to hide beauty.

questions.q: Who enforces equality, and how does the story end for Harrison?
questions.a: Diana Moon Glampers, the Handicapper General, shoots Harrison and the ballerina with a shotgun on live TV.

days.guide: Record a 15-minute discussion: does the story mock equality or forced sameness? Each side cites three lines.

questions.q: Why do George and Hazel forget Harrison's death so quickly?
questions.a: Their handicaps (and Hazel's average mind) keep them from holding thoughts — Vonnegut shows how forced sameness destroys feeling and memory.

days.guide: Read 'The Story of an Hour' twice; annotate window imagery and the final line.

questions.q: What does Louise see through the open window, and what does it symbolize?
questions.a: Spring life — trees, patches of blue sky, sounds of life — symbolizing the new freedom opening before her.

questions.q: Explain the irony of the last line.
questions.a: Doctors say she died 'of the joy that kills' (joy at Brently being alive), but she actually died from the shock of losing her freedom.

days.guide: Your child picks a story from Units 1–2, drafts three thesis statements, chooses the strongest, and outlines body paragraphs.

questions.q: Which is a stronger thesis: 'The Necklace is about a necklace' or 'In The Necklace, Maupassant shows that pride turns a small mistake into a lifetime of suffering'?
questions.a: The second — it is specific and arguable.

days.guide: Collect the outline and evidence chart; give the reading check.

questions.q: What does Louise whisper repeatedly in her room?
questions.a: 'Free! Body and soul free!' (also 'free, free, free!').

weeks.assessment_key: Outline/evidence review: proficient = arguable thesis about theme, three body topics that each support it, six relevant quotations with page numbers and a note on how each supports the claim. Reading check answers: 1) Harrison is 14 (and 7 feet tall). 2) Year: 2081. 3) The Handicapper General is Diana Moon Glampers. 4) George's handicap: mental radio and weights. 5) Louise Mallard learns of Brently's death in a railroad accident. 6) Her sister Josephine and husband's friend Richards tell her. 7) Brently returns alive. 8) She dies of heart disease.

weeks.prep: Outline from Week 7, the Purdue OWL MLA page on in-text citations, and three model introductions (from CommonLit or online writing samples).
misconceptions: Dropping quotations in without introduction: embed them in your own sentence with a signal phrase.
Commentary that just repeats the quote: explain HOW the words prove the claim (focus on specific word choices).
Conclusions that only restate: extend — why does this theme matter?

days.guide: Compare three model introductions. Your child writes hook, context (title, author, situation), and thesis.

questions.q: What three parts should a literary analysis introduction contain?
questions.a: A hook, brief context (title, author, situation of the story), and an arguable thesis.

days.guide: Model a claim–evidence–commentary paragraph with an embedded quotation and MLA citation (Author page). Your child drafts two body paragraphs.

questions.q: Fix the citation: As Poe says 'I drink to your long life'. (pg. 4)
questions.a: Montresor toasts, "I drink to your long life" (Poe 4).

days.guide: Draft the last body paragraph and a conclusion (900–1,100 words total).

questions.q: What should a conclusion do beyond restating the thesis?
questions.a: Extend the idea — explain why the theme matters or how it connects beyond the story.

days.guide: Revise transitions and verbs; edit quotation punctuation.

questions.q: Replace 'shows' with three more precise analytical verbs.
questions.a: Reveals, underscores, emphasizes (also suggests, exposes, highlights).

days.guide: Collect the final essay. Give a 45-minute timed write on an unseen excerpt.

questions.q: In a timed write, what should you do in the first 5 minutes?
questions.a: Read the prompt and passage, annotate, and jot a thesis and two supporting points.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = precise, arguable thesis; logically ordered body paragraphs each with a topic sentence, embedded quotations cited correctly, and commentary that explains significance; effective transitions; conclusion extends the idea; few errors. 3 = clear thesis, adequate evidence and explanation, some summary, minor errors. 2 = vague thesis, evidence thin or poorly explained, organization uneven. 1 = no clear thesis, little evidence, errors interfere. Timed write: same rubric scaled for a draft; proficient = clear claim about the excerpt, at least two quoted details, explanation of their effect.

weeks.prep: Find texts and videos: Patrick Henry's 'Speech to the Virginia Convention' (1775) and JFK's 1961 Inaugural Address (JFK Library website has video). Collect 10 ads from magazines or online.
misconceptions: Thinking logos means 'logical-sounding': logos is an appeal using facts, statistics, and reasoning.
Confusing antithesis with any contrast: antithesis places opposing ideas in parallel structure ('Ask not... ask...').
Naming devices without explaining their effect on the audience.

days.guide: Teach speaker–audience–purpose and ethos, pathos, logos. Your child labels appeals in 10 ads.

questions.q: An ad says '9 out of 10 dentists recommend our toothpaste.' Which appeal?
questions.a: Logos (statistic) — with some ethos (dentists' authority).

days.guide: Read Henry's speech; annotate rhetorical questions and emotional appeals.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Henry's speech?
questions.a: To persuade the Virginia Convention to prepare for armed resistance against Britain.

questions.q: Explain the effect of 'Is life so dear, or peace so sweet, as to be purchased at the price of chains and slavery?'
questions.a: The rhetorical question frames peace with Britain as slavery, stirring emotion (pathos) and making resistance seem the only honorable choice.

days.guide: Watch and read JFK's Inaugural; find antithesis and parallelism.

questions.q: Identify the device in 'Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country.'
questions.a: Antithesis (and chiasmus) — reversed, contrasting ideas in parallel form.

days.guide: Complete a SOAPSTone chart (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone) for one speech; write a rhetorical analysis paragraph.

questions.q: SOAPSTone for JFK's Inaugural: occasion and audience?
questions.a: Occasion: his inauguration, January 20, 1961, during the Cold War. Audience: Americans and the world, including allies and adversaries.

days.guide: Your child gives a 2-minute oral analysis of a device; give the term quiz.

questions.q: Define parallelism.
questions.a: Repeating the same grammatical structure for related ideas (e.g., 'pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship').

weeks.assessment_key: Rhetorical paragraph: Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence. Oral explanation: 4 = names device, quotes it, explains effect on audience clearly in 2 minutes with eye contact. Term quiz answers: ethos = credibility; pathos = emotion; logos = logic/evidence; rhetorical question = question asked for effect, not answer; antithesis = contrasting ideas in parallel structure; parallelism = repeated grammatical structure; anaphora = repetition at the start of clauses; tone = speaker's attitude.

weeks.prep: Print 'A Call for Unity' (1963) and King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (King Institute at Stanford has the text). Read both first; the Letter is long (about 7,000 words), so plan reading in thirds. Brief background: the 1963 Birmingham campaign against segregation; King was jailed on April 12, 1963, for violating an injunction against demonstrating.
misconceptions: Thinking King rejects all law: he argues one must obey just laws and openly, lovingly, and with willingness to accept the penalty, break unjust ones.
Seeing the Letter as purely emotional: it is tightly reasoned (logos), with ethos and pathos layered in.
Missing the audience: King addresses the clergymen (and white moderates) respectfully while refuting them.

days.guide: Read 'A Call for Unity'; your child summarizes the clergymen's objections and notes the context.

questions.q: What do the clergymen call the demonstrations?
questions.a: 'Unwise and untimely'; they urged people to rely on the courts and negotiation and criticized 'outsiders' for leading them.

days.guide: Read the first third; chart each criticism and King's reasoning.

questions.q: How does King answer the charge that he is an outsider?
questions.a: He was invited by an affiliate organization, and 'I am in Birmingham because injustice is here'; 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.'

questions.q: What are the four basic steps of a nonviolent campaign King lists?
questions.a: Collection of the facts to determine whether injustices exist; negotiation; self-purification; and direct action.

days.guide: Read the middle section; your child explains just vs. unjust laws with two quotations.

questions.q: How does King define a just law and an unjust law?
questions.a: A just law 'squares with the moral law or the law of God'; an unjust law is 'out of harmony with the moral law.' Any law that uplifts human personality is just; any law that degrades it is unjust.

days.guide: Finish the Letter; analyze how King balances patience and urgency; evaluate his strongest evidence.

questions.q: What does King say about the word 'Wait'?
questions.a: That 'Wait' has almost always meant 'Never,' and that 'justice too long delayed is justice denied.'

questions.q: Why is King 'gravely disappointed with the white moderate'?
questions.a: Because the moderate prefers order ('the absence of tension') to justice and tells Black citizens to wait for a 'more convenient season.'

days.guide: Your child writes a one-page analysis: How does King refute the charge of 'untimely'?

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence King uses to show the action is not untimely.
questions.a: Examples: Black Americans have waited more than 340 years for rights; the long sentence describing lynch mobs, police brutality, and explaining segregation to a child shows why waiting is unbearable.

weeks.assessment_key: One-page analysis rubric: 4 = identifies the clergymen's 'untimely' charge, traces King's counterargument ('Wait' means 'Never'; 340 years of waiting; the long sentence of grievances; freedom is never voluntarily given by the oppressor), evaluates why his evidence is persuasive, and quotes accurately; 3 = traces the argument with less evaluation; 2 = mostly summary; 1 = inaccurate or no evidence.

weeks.prep: Print the Declaration's preamble, the Gettysburg Address, and an excerpt of Douglass's 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (1852). Make a list of 8 fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, slippery slope, bandwagon, hasty generalization, appeal to authority, red herring) with examples.
misconceptions: Using 'all men are created equal' only as a quote: Lincoln and Douglass both use it as a standard to judge the nation.
Calling any weak argument 'ad hominem': ad hominem specifically attacks the person instead of the argument.
Choosing a research issue that isn't debatable (e.g., 'pollution is bad').

days.guide: Read the preamble and Gettysburg Address; your child lists ideas Lincoln echoes and how he redefines them.

questions.q: Which idea from the Declaration does Lincoln echo in his first sentence?
questions.a: That the nation was 'dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.'

questions.q: How does Lincoln redefine the war's purpose?
questions.a: As a test of whether a nation founded on equality can endure, calling for 'a new birth of freedom' and government 'of the people, by the people, for the people.'

days.guide: Read the Douglass excerpt; analyze how he uses the Declaration's ideals to indict slavery.

questions.q: What does Douglass say the Fourth of July reveals to the American slave?
questions.a: 'More than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.'

questions.q: How does Douglass use the nation's ideals against it?
questions.a: He praises the founders' principles, then shows that slavery betrays them, making the celebration hypocritical ('This Fourth of July is yours, not mine').

days.guide: Teach 8 fallacies; your child identifies them in 12 samples.

questions.q: 'Either we ban phones in school or students will never learn anything.' Name the fallacy.
questions.a: False dilemma (either/or).

questions.q: 'Everyone is buying these shoes, so you should too.' Name the fallacy.
questions.a: Bandwagon.

days.guide: Your child picks an issue, finds two credible sources, and logs claims and evidence.

questions.q: What makes a source credible for a research log?
questions.a: Known, accountable author or organization; evidence and citations; current; purpose to inform rather than sell; confirmed by other sources.

days.guide: Fallacy quiz; your child writes a claim plus three reasons.

questions.q: 'My opponent didn't even go to college, so his tax plan is wrong.' Fallacy?
questions.a: Ad hominem.

weeks.assessment_key: Document comparison chart: proficient = notes 'all men are created equal' and liberty in all three; Lincoln reframes equality as the nation's unfinished task; Douglass uses it to expose slavery's hypocrisy. Fallacy quiz answers (sample items): 1) 'If we allow one late assignment, soon no one will turn anything in' — slippery slope. 2) 'You think we should fund schools more? So you want to waste money' — straw man. 3) 'A famous actor says this vitamin works' — false appeal to authority. 4) 'Two teens I know are rude, so all teens are rude' — hasty generalization. 5) Changing the subject to avoid the question — red herring. Claim approved if debatable, specific, and supported by three distinct reasons.

weeks.prep: Research log and two sources. A parallel-structure worksheet (10 faulty sentences). Prepare the Unit 3 test on rhetoric and argument.
misconceptions: Weak counterclaims (a straw man): state the opposing view fairly and in its strongest form before rebutting.
Evidence without reasoning: explain how each statistic or quote supports the claim.
Faulty parallelism such as 'I like hiking, to swim, and biking' → 'hiking, swimming, and biking.'

days.guide: Your child writes an introduction with context and a precise claim, then one cited body paragraph.

questions.q: Make this claim more precise: 'School should start later.'
questions.a: Sample: 'High schools in our district should start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. because later start times improve teen sleep, attendance, and safety.'

days.guide: Draft the counterclaim-rebuttal paragraph.

questions.q: What are the two parts of a counterclaim paragraph?
questions.a: A fair statement of the opposing view (with its reasoning), then a rebuttal using evidence and reasoning.

days.guide: Fix 10 faulty parallel sentences; revise the essay to include two deliberate parallel structures.

questions.q: Fix: 'The coach told us to stretch, hydrating, and that we should rest.'
questions.a: 'The coach told us to stretch, hydrate, and rest.'

days.guide: Finish, revise, and edit the 800–1,000-word essay; check citations.

questions.q: Where should in-text citations appear for paraphrased evidence?
questions.a: Right after the paraphrased information, in parentheses (author's last name and page if available), even when not quoting.

days.guide: Hold a 10-minute mini-debate; submit the essay; give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: In a debate, what should a rebuttal do?
questions.a: Directly address the opponent's point and explain with evidence why it is weaker than your argument.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument essay rubric (W.9-10.1): 4 = precise claim, logically sequenced reasons with relevant cited evidence, fair counterclaim with convincing rebuttal, formal tone, strong conclusion, correct MLA; 3 = clear claim and evidence, counterclaim present but thin; 2 = claim unclear or evidence weak, no real counterclaim; 1 = opinion without support. Debate checklist: states claim, uses evidence, listens and responds to opponent, respectful tone. Unit 3 test sample answers: 1) Henry's purpose — rally armed resistance. 2) JFK 'Ask not…' — antithesis/chiasmus. 3) King: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere' — answers the 'outsider' charge. 4) King's just law definition. 5) Douglass — the Fourth reveals injustice to the slave. 6) Identify fallacies in three items. 7) Short analysis of an unseen paragraph's appeals.

weeks.prep: Print Dickinson's 'Hope is the thing with feathers' and Frost's 'The Road Not Taken' and 'Nothing Gold Can Stay' (Poetry Foundation). Prepare a TP-CASTT template (Title, Paraphrase, Connotation, Attitude, Shifts, Title again, Theme) and 20 connotation pairs.
misconceptions: Reading 'The Road Not Taken' as simple praise of nonconformity: the speaker says the roads were 'really about the same'; the 'sigh' and future retelling suggest we create meaning for our choices afterward.
Ignoring the speaker: the poet and speaker aren't necessarily the same person.
Treating connotation as definition: connotation is the emotional association (thrifty = positive, stingy = negative).

days.guide: Read the poem twice. Your child maps each part of the bird metaphor to hope.

questions.q: What qualities of hope does Dickinson show through the bird?
questions.a: It lives in the soul ('perches in the soul'), sings constantly without words, is sweetest in hardship ('in the Gale'), survives in 'the chillest land,' and never asks anything in return ('It asked a crumb — of me').

days.guide: Read 'The Road Not Taken' twice; debate the common misreading using the final stanza.

questions.q: What does the speaker say about how worn the two roads were?
questions.a: They were worn 'really about the same' — neither was clearly less traveled.

questions.q: How does the last stanza support the 'misreading' interpretation?
questions.a: The speaker imagines telling the story 'with a sigh' 'ages and ages hence,' claiming he took 'the one less traveled by' — suggesting he will reshape the memory to give the choice meaning.

days.guide: Read 'Nothing Gold Can Stay'; annotate allusion and imagery; complete TP-CASTT.

questions.q: What allusion appears in the poem, and what does it add?
questions.a: 'So Eden sank to grief' — the biblical Garden of Eden; it expands the theme from leaves to the human loss of innocence.

questions.q: State the theme.
questions.a: Beauty, youth, and innocence are precious but brief; all perfect moments fade.

days.guide: Sort 20 word pairs by connotation; your child rewrites a stanza swapping connotations to change tone.

questions.q: Give the connotation of 'confident' vs. 'arrogant.'
questions.a: Confident = positive (self-assured); arrogant = negative (overly proud).

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph analyzing a figurative device in an unseen Dickinson poem (e.g., 'Because I could not stop for Death').

questions.q: In 'Because I could not stop for Death,' how is Death personified?
questions.a: As a kind, patient gentleman caller who gives the speaker a carriage ride.

weeks.assessment_key: TP-CASTT chart for 'Nothing Gold Can Stay' — proficient: Paraphrase: new leaves first appear golden like blossoms but soon become ordinary green; Eden fell; dawn becomes day. Connotation: gold = precious; 'subsides,' 'sank,' 'goes down' = decline. Attitude: wistful, accepting. Shift: line 6 moves from nature to Eden/humanity. Theme: precious beginnings never last. Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence.

weeks.prep: Print Sonnets 18 and 130, Hughes's 'Harlem' and 'Mother to Son,' and Dunbar's 'We Wear the Mask.' Review iambic pentameter (da-DUM ×5) and the Shakespearean form (3 quatrains + couplet, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG).
misconceptions: Thinking Sonnet 130 insults the speaker's love: it mocks exaggerated poetic comparisons and ends by declaring his love 'as rare' as any.
Marking stress by syllable count only: say the line aloud to hear natural stresses.
Reading 'We Wear the Mask' as about individuals only: Dunbar writes about African Americans hiding pain from a society that doesn't want to see it.

days.guide: Scan line 1 of Sonnet 18 together; mark rhyme scheme and volta; your child paraphrases each quatrain.

questions.q: What is the rhyme scheme of Sonnet 18 and where is the volta?
questions.a: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG; the volta comes at line 9, 'But thy eternal summer shall not fade.'

questions.q: What does the couplet claim?
questions.a: As long as people live and read, this poem will live and give the beloved life — the poem makes her beauty immortal.

days.guide: Read Sonnet 130; compare with 18 in a Venn diagram.

questions.q: What does 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun' do to traditional love poetry?
questions.a: It parodies the exaggerated comparisons poets use; the couplet says his love is as rare as any woman 'belied with false compare.'

days.guide: Read both Hughes poems; explain similes and the staircase metaphor.

questions.q: What similes describe a deferred dream in 'Harlem'?
questions.a: It might 'dry up like a raisin in the sun,' 'fester like a sore,' 'stink like rotten meat,' 'crust and sugar over like a syrupy sweet,' or 'sag like a heavy load' — or explode.

questions.q: What does 'Life for me ain't been no crystal stair' mean?
questions.a: Her life has been hard — full of 'tacks,' 'splinters,' and 'boards torn up' — but she keeps 'climbin'' and urges her son not to quit.

days.guide: Read 'We Wear the Mask'; analyze the rondeau form and refrain; connect to Hughes.

questions.q: What does the mask hide, according to Dunbar?
questions.a: Pain and suffering ('torn and bleeding hearts'); the mask 'grins and lies' so the world sees only smiles.

questions.q: What is the effect of the refrain 'We wear the mask'?
questions.a: Repetition emphasizes the constant, unavoidable nature of hiding pain.

days.guide: Poetic-terms/scansion quiz; comparative paragraph on form.

questions.q: How many syllables in a line of iambic pentameter?
questions.a: Ten (five iambs).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) iamb = unstressed-stressed. 2) pentameter = five feet. 3) Shakespearean sonnet = 14 lines, 3 quatrains + couplet. 4) volta = turn. 5) refrain = repeated line. 6) Scan 'Shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY' (shall I / com-PARE / thee TO / a SUM / mer's DAY). 7) Rhyme scheme of Sonnet 130 = ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. 8) Simile vs. metaphor definitions. Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence.

weeks.prep: Bookmark the Poetry Out Loud anthology (poetryoutloud.org). Recording device. Print the Poetry Out Loud evaluation criteria (physical presence, voice and articulation, dramatic appropriateness, evidence of understanding, accuracy). Prepare the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Over-acting a recitation: the poem's meaning should lead; let the words carry the drama.
Analysis essays that list devices: connect each device to how it builds the theme.
Ending lines randomly in free verse: line breaks should create emphasis or pause.

days.guide: Your child browses and chooses a 14–25 line poem, marks pauses and emphasis, and begins memorizing (stanza by stanza).

questions.q: What is a good strategy for memorizing a poem?
questions.a: Learn a few lines at a time, say them aloud repeatedly, add lines cumulatively, and practice from memory daily.

days.guide: Your child writes a 600-word analysis explaining how two devices build the theme.

questions.q: What should each body paragraph in the analysis include?
questions.a: A claim about one device, quotations from the poem, and an explanation of how that device builds the theme.

days.guide: Your child writes an original sonnet or free-verse poem built on an extended metaphor; revise line breaks.

questions.q: What is an extended metaphor?
questions.a: A comparison developed over several lines or a whole poem (like Dickinson's hope as a bird).

days.guide: Rehearse with attention to volume, pacing, and eye contact; record and self-critique.

questions.q: Name two Poetry Out Loud evaluation criteria.
questions.a: Any two: physical presence, voice and articulation, dramatic appropriateness, evidence of understanding, accuracy.

days.guide: Recitation for family or recorded; submit analysis and poem; give the Unit 4 test.

questions.q: What is a dramatic monologue?
questions.a: A poem spoken by one character to a silent listener, revealing the speaker's personality.

weeks.assessment_key: Recitation scoring (1–6 per Poetry Out Loud criterion; proficient ≈ 4+): physical presence, voice/articulation, dramatic appropriateness, evidence of understanding, accuracy (fewer than 2 prompts). Analysis essay: Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = precise, arguable thesis; logically ordered body paragraphs each with a topic sentence, embedded quotations cited correctly, and commentary that explains significance; effective transitions; conclusion extends the idea; few errors. 3 = clear thesis, adequate evidence and explanation, some summary, minor errors. 2 = vague thesis, evidence thin or poorly explained, organization uneven. 1 = no clear thesis, little evidence, errors interfere. Original poem: 4 = sustained extended metaphor, purposeful line breaks, vivid imagery. Unit 4 test sample answers: Dickinson's bird = hope; 'The Road Not Taken' roads worn 'about the same'; Eden allusion in Frost; Sonnet 18 volta line 9; Sonnet 130 parodies conventions; 'Harlem' similes; 'Mother to Son' staircase metaphor; Dunbar's refrain.

weeks.prep: Get The Odyssey (Butler translation free, or Fagles/Fitzgerald from the library) and a Mediterranean map. Read Books 1 and 5 first and a short background article (oral tradition, Trojan War, Homer). Note: translations differ in wording — let your child cite their edition.
misconceptions: Thinking the poem begins at the beginning of the journey: it starts in medias res, ten years after Troy, with Odysseus stranded.
Seeing xenia as simple politeness: guest-friendship was a sacred obligation protected by Zeus.
Assuming Odysseus is purely heroic: Homer presents a clever but flawed hero.

days.guide: Read the background article and map key stops (Troy, Ithaca, the Cyclops' island, Circe's island, Calypso's Ogygia, Phaeacia).

questions.q: What war is Odysseus returning from, and how long has he been gone?
questions.a: The Trojan War; the war took ten years and his journey home another ten — twenty years in all.

days.guide: Read Book 1; identify the invocation, in medias res, Telemachus, and the suitors.

questions.q: What is the invocation?
questions.a: The opening prayer asking the Muse to sing the story of the man 'of many ways/twists and turns.'

questions.q: What problem do Penelope and Telemachus face in Ithaca?
questions.a: Suitors are living in Odysseus's house, eating his wealth, and pressuring Penelope to remarry.

days.guide: Track xenia in Book 1.

questions.q: How does Telemachus show xenia to Athena (disguised as Mentes)?
questions.a: He welcomes the stranger, takes the spear, seats and feeds the guest before asking who he is.

days.guide: Read Book 5; analyze Odysseus's choice to leave Calypso.

questions.q: Why does Odysseus leave Calypso even though she offers immortality?
questions.a: He longs for home, Ithaca, and Penelope; he chooses mortal life and identity over endless life with her.

days.guide: Quiz on epic conventions and Books 1 and 5; notebook entry on Greek values.

questions.q: Who orders Calypso to release Odysseus?
questions.a: Zeus, through the messenger god Hermes (at Athena's request).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Epic = long narrative poem about a hero's deeds. 2) Invocation = appeal to the Muse. 3) In medias res = beginning in the middle. 4) Epithet example: 'grey-eyed Athena' / 'rosy-fingered Dawn'. 5) Athena disguises herself as Mentes. 6) Suitors are consuming Odysseus's estate. 7) Calypso holds Odysseus on Ogygia for seven years. 8) Hermes delivers Zeus's command. 9) Poseidon wrecks Odysseus's raft. 10) He washes ashore in Phaeacia. Notebook entry proficient: names values such as hospitality (xenia), loyalty, cleverness, honor, and respect for the gods with examples.

weeks.prep: Odyssey Books 9–10. Prepare a cause-effect chain template and the seminar rubric (prepared, cites text, builds on others, asks questions).
misconceptions: Thinking blinding the Cyclops causes all of Odysseus's troubles: it's his boast revealing his name that lets Polyphemus curse him through Poseidon.
Equating 'hubris' with any pride: hubris is excessive pride that defies the gods or limits and brings punishment.
Judging leadership only by results: weigh decisions, care for men, and mistakes.

days.guide: Read Book 9 (Cyclops); your child lists clever choices and mistakes.

questions.q: What clever trick does Odysseus use with his name?
questions.a: He tells Polyphemus his name is 'Nobody,' so when Polyphemus cries that 'Nobody' is hurting him, the other Cyclopes don't help.

questions.q: Name one mistake Odysseus makes in the cave episode.
questions.a: Staying in the cave to see the owner and gain gifts despite his men urging them to leave (or later boasting his real name).

days.guide: Analyze the boast and its consequences in a cause-effect chain.

questions.q: What happens because Odysseus shouts his real name?
questions.a: Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon to curse Odysseus — that he reach home late, alone, having lost all his men, and find trouble at home.

days.guide: Read Book 10; compare Odysseus's leadership with Book 9.

questions.q: What happens with Aeolus's bag of winds?
questions.a: Within sight of Ithaca, while Odysseus sleeps, the crew opens the bag thinking it holds treasure; the winds blow them back.

questions.q: How does Odysseus overcome Circe?
questions.a: Hermes gives him the herb moly to resist her drugs; he forces her to restore his men.

days.guide: Your child writes three open-ended leadership questions with text references.

questions.q: Example of an open-ended seminar question?
questions.a: 'Is Odysseus responsible for the loss of his men, or are they responsible for their own fates? Use Books 9 and 10.'

days.guide: Hold a 20-minute seminar on whether Odysseus is a good leader; your child writes a reflection.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence that Odysseus is a good leader.
questions.a: He devises the escape under the rams' bellies and saves the surviving men from the Cyclops (or goes alone to rescue men from Circe).

weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric: 4 = cites specific episodes from Books 9–10, weighs both sides, builds on others' points, asks a deepening question; 3 = participates with some evidence; 2 = opinions without evidence; 1 = minimal participation. Reflection proficient: takes a position on Odysseus's leadership supported by at least two specific episodes and acknowledges a counterpoint.

weeks.prep: Odyssey Books 11–12; a semester review packet (literary terms, rhetorical devices, short practice passages). Plan a 2-hour exam block for Day 5.
misconceptions: Thinking Odysseus loses his last crew because of Scylla: the crew dies after eating Helios's sacred cattle against his warning.
Reading the Sirens as only literal monsters: they also represent temptation and dangerous knowledge.
Forgetting that Books 9–12 are Odysseus's story told at the Phaeacian court (a flashback).

days.guide: Read Book 11; explain Tiresias's prophecy and Achilles's words about glory.

questions.q: What does Tiresias warn Odysseus about?
questions.a: Not to harm the cattle of the sun god Helios; if they do, his crew will be destroyed and he will return home late and alone to find trouble in his house.

questions.q: What does Achilles say about death and glory?
questions.a: He would rather be a poor laborer/servant on earth than king over all the dead — challenging the value of glory.

days.guide: Read Book 12; discuss what each hazard represents.

questions.q: How does Odysseus get past the Sirens?
questions.a: He plugs his men's ears with beeswax and has himself tied to the mast so he can hear the song safely.

questions.q: Why does Odysseus choose Scylla over Charybdis?
questions.a: Charybdis's whirlpool could destroy the whole ship; Scylla takes only six men.

days.guide: Explain how the flashback structure builds suspense for the return.

questions.q: Why does Homer tell Books 9–12 as a flashback?
questions.a: We meet Odysseus near the end of his journey and learn his past through his own story, which deepens his character and builds anticipation for his return to Ithaca.

days.guide: Review terms and complete practice passages.

questions.q: Define dramatic irony and give an example from this semester.
questions.a: When the audience knows something characters don't — e.g., the reader knows Montresor's plan while Fortunato doesn't.

days.guide: Give the semester exam: unseen story and nonfiction passages plus a timed analytical essay.

questions.q: What should a timed analytical essay thesis contain?
questions.a: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and previews the main points.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam: reading questions scored right/wrong (80%+ proficient); timed essay with the rubric. Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = precise, arguable thesis; logically ordered body paragraphs each with a topic sentence, embedded quotations cited correctly, and commentary that explains significance; effective transitions; conclusion extends the idea; few errors. 3 = clear thesis, adequate evidence and explanation, some summary, minor errors. 2 = vague thesis, evidence thin or poorly explained, organization uneven. 1 = no clear thesis, little evidence, errors interfere. Sample term answers: irony types, conflict types, theme statement, ethos/pathos/logos, antithesis, epic conventions, in medias res, xenia.

weeks.prep: Odyssey Books 13–16. Prepare a 'Telemachus then and now' chart.
misconceptions: Thinking Odysseus reveals himself immediately: he stays disguised to test loyalty and plan.
Overlooking Eumaeus: a humble swineherd shows the truest xenia and loyalty.
Treating Telemachus as unchanged: by Book 16 he is acting like a leader.

days.guide: Read Book 13; explain Athena's disguise and its purpose.

questions.q: Why does Athena disguise Odysseus as an old beggar?
questions.a: So he can enter his home safely, test who is loyal, and plan revenge on the suitors without being recognized.

days.guide: Read Book 14; analyze Eumaeus.

questions.q: How does Eumaeus show xenia and loyalty?
questions.a: He welcomes and feeds the ragged stranger before knowing who he is and stays loyal to his absent master, mourning him and resenting the suitors.

days.guide: Read Books 15–16; chart Telemachus's change since Book 1.

questions.q: How has Telemachus changed since Book 1?
questions.a: He has gone from a passive, uncertain youth to one who traveled to seek news, avoided the suitors' ambush, and is ready to act with his father.

days.guide: Your child writes a scene analysis of the reunion with three quotations.

questions.q: Why doesn't Telemachus believe Odysseus at first?
questions.a: Athena has transformed him so dramatically that Telemachus thinks he must be a god.

days.guide: Reading quiz; vocabulary-in-context check.

questions.q: Where does the father-son reunion take place?
questions.a: In Eumaeus's hut.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) The Phaeacians carry sleeping Odysseus to Ithaca. 2) Athena disguises him as a beggar. 3) Eumaeus is the loyal swineherd. 4) Telemachus returns from Sparta/Pylos and avoids the suitors' ambush. 5) Reunion in Eumaeus's hut. 6) They plan to kill the suitors. Scene analysis: Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence.

weeks.prep: Odyssey Books 17–23 (selected). Parental note: Book 22 is violent (the slaughter of the suitors and the hanging of disloyal maids) — preview and discuss.
misconceptions: Thinking Penelope is passive: she outwits the suitors (the shroud trick) and tests Odysseus herself.
Judging the revenge only by modern standards — or ignoring them: discuss both Greek ideas of justice (xenia violated) and whether the punishment is excessive.
Mixing up the bow test and the bed test: the bow contest proves Odysseus's strength to the suitors; the bed proves his identity to Penelope.

days.guide: Read Books 17–18; note how the suitors treat the beggar.

questions.q: How do the suitors violate xenia toward the beggar?
questions.a: They insult and mock him; Antinous throws a footstool at him; they deny him proper hospitality.

questions.q: What happens to Odysseus's dog, Argos?
questions.a: Old and neglected, Argos recognizes his master, wags his tail, and dies.

days.guide: Read Books 19 and 21; analyze Penelope's intelligence.

questions.q: How did Penelope delay the suitors?
questions.a: She said she would remarry when she finished weaving a shroud for Laertes, and secretly unraveled it each night.

questions.q: Who recognizes Odysseus by his scar, and what is the contest?
questions.a: His old nurse Eurycleia; the contest is to string Odysseus's bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axe heads.

days.guide: Read Book 22; your child debates in writing whether the revenge is justice or excess.

questions.q: Whom does Odysseus kill first?
questions.a: Antinous, the most arrogant suitor.

days.guide: Read Book 23; explain the bed test.

questions.q: How does Penelope test Odysseus with the bed?
questions.a: She tells the nurse to move their bed; Odysseus angrily says it can't be moved because he built it around a living olive tree — a secret only they knew.

questions.q: Why does this make Penelope Odysseus's equal?
questions.a: She uses his own kind of cunning and disguise to test him.

days.guide: Family discussion on justice; Penelope character chart.

questions.q: Name two of Penelope's character traits with evidence.
questions.a: Clever (shroud trick, bed test) and loyal (waits twenty years).

weeks.assessment_key: Discussion notes: proficient = at least two cited episodes and a reasoned view on justice vs. excess. Penelope chart (proficient): traits — cunning (shroud, bed), loyal (twenty years), cautious (tests the stranger), grieving/emotional (weeps for Odysseus) — each with a book reference.

weeks.prep: Print Tennyson's 'Ulysses.' Prepare an essay planner. Prepare the Unit 5 test on the Odyssey.
misconceptions: Assuming Tennyson's Ulysses is content at home: he is restless and wants to sail again.
Essays that retell the plot: each body paragraph should argue one heroic quality.
Using evidence from only one or two books: require at least four.

days.guide: Read the monologue aloud; compare with Homer's homecoming.

questions.q: How does Tennyson's Ulysses feel about being home?
questions.a: Restless and bored — 'It little profits that an idle king, / By this still hearth' — he wants to travel and 'drink life to the lees.'

questions.q: What is the poem's final line?
questions.a: 'To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.'

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph on how and why Tennyson transforms Homer's hero.

questions.q: How does Tennyson's hero differ from Homer's?
questions.a: Homer's hero longs for home; Tennyson's, once home, longs for adventure and continued striving even in old age.

days.guide: Plan the essay on Odysseus as an epic hero.

questions.q: Name three epic-hero qualities Odysseus shows.
questions.a: Cleverness (Trojan horse, 'Nobody'), courage/endurance (Sirens, twenty years), loyalty/devotion to home (leaves Calypso) — also flaws like pride.

days.guide: Draft the 800-word essay with evidence from at least four books.

questions.q: How do you cite the Odyssey?
questions.a: By book and line number (or page) depending on the translation, e.g., (Homer 9.502).

days.guide: Revise, edit, submit; Unit 5 test.

questions.q: Who is Tiresias?
questions.a: The blind prophet Odysseus consults in the Underworld.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = precise, arguable thesis; logically ordered body paragraphs each with a topic sentence, embedded quotations cited correctly, and commentary that explains significance; effective transitions; conclusion extends the idea; few errors. 3 = clear thesis, adequate evidence and explanation, some summary, minor errors. 2 = vague thesis, evidence thin or poorly explained, organization uneven. 1 = no clear thesis, little evidence, errors interfere. Unit 5 test answers (sample): invocation; in medias res; xenia examples; 'Nobody' trick; hubris boast; Circe and moly; Tiresias's warning about Helios's cattle; Sirens and wax; Scylla vs. Charybdis; Eumaeus; Argos; the bow and axes; the olive-tree bed; Tennyson's 'To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.'

weeks.prep: Bookmark the Folger free online Romeo and Juliet. Watch a short Globe Theatre video. Make a glossary card: wherefore = why; anon = soon; hie = hurry; ere = before; thou/thee = you; art = are; hath = has; marry = indeed; 'tis = it is.
misconceptions: 'Wherefore art thou Romeo' means 'why are you Romeo' (a Montague), not 'where are you.'
Expecting suspense from 'what happens': the Prologue reveals the ending; suspense comes from how and why.
Reading every line literally: Shakespeare's characters pun constantly (Mercutio, Sampson and Gregory).

days.guide: Introduce the Globe, groundlings, and Shakespeare's language; your child translates 15 words.

questions.q: What does 'wherefore' mean?
questions.a: Why.

days.guide: Read and paraphrase the Prologue sonnet; predict how knowing the ending affects suspense.

questions.q: What does the Prologue reveal about the lovers?
questions.a: They are 'star-crossed' lovers from two feuding households in Verona whose deaths will end the feud.

days.guide: Read 1.1–1.3; mark puns and insults.

questions.q: How does the brawl start in 1.1?
questions.a: Capulet servants Sampson and Gregory provoke Montague servants (biting the thumb); a fight breaks out, Tybalt joins, and the Prince threatens death for further fighting.

questions.q: Whom does Romeo love at the start?
questions.a: Rosaline, who doesn't return his love.

days.guide: Read 1.4–1.5; analyze Queen Mab and the shared sonnet.

questions.q: What image system do Romeo and Juliet use in their first conversation?
questions.a: Religious imagery — pilgrims, saints, holy shrine, prayer — forming a shared sonnet.

questions.q: What does Juliet say on learning Romeo is a Montague?
questions.a: 'My only love sprung from my only hate!'

days.guide: Act 1 quiz; paraphrase 20 lines.

questions.q: Who recognizes Romeo at the party and wants to fight?
questions.a: Tybalt; Lord Capulet stops him.

weeks.assessment_key: Act 1 quiz answers: 1) Setting: Verona. 2) Prince's decree: death for future street fighting. 3) Romeo loves Rosaline at first. 4) Paris wants to marry Juliet. 5) Juliet is not yet 14. 6) Mercutio gives the Queen Mab speech. 7) Romeo and Juliet meet at the Capulets' feast. 8) Tybalt recognizes Romeo's voice. 9) Shared sonnet uses pilgrim/saint imagery. 10) 'My only love sprung from my only hate.' Paraphrase rubric: accurate meaning, modern English, no lines skipped.

weeks.prep: R&J Act 2. A light/dark imagery chart. Recruit family for reading parts.
misconceptions: 'What's in a name?' doesn't mean names are unimportant to the play: Juliet wishes the name Montague didn't matter — but the feud makes it matter fatally.
Seeing the Friar as purely wise: he warns 'Wisely and slow' yet rushes the marriage for political hopes.
Thinking Juliet is as impulsive as Romeo in 2.2: she voices caution ('too rash, too unadvised, too sudden').

days.guide: Read 2.2 aloud; chart light/dark imagery.

questions.q: What metaphor does Romeo use when he sees Juliet at the window?
questions.a: 'It is the east, and Juliet is the sun' — she is light that outshines everything.

days.guide: Analyze Juliet's caution with two lines.

questions.q: Quote a line where Juliet is cautious.
questions.a: 'It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden, / Too like the lightning' — or 'O, swear not by the moon, th' inconstant moon.'

days.guide: Read 2.3; explain 'Wisely and slow' and the Friar's reasons.

questions.q: Why does Friar Laurence agree to marry them?
questions.a: He hopes the marriage will turn the households' 'rancor to pure love' — end the feud.

questions.q: What does 'Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast' warn?
questions.a: Rushing leads to mistakes.

days.guide: Read 2.4–2.6; perform a short scene with family.

questions.q: What does the Friar warn in 2.6?
questions.a: 'These violent delights have violent ends' — intense passion can end in disaster.

days.guide: Act 2 quiz; journal: Who is most responsible for the rush to marry?

questions.q: Who carries messages between Romeo and Juliet?
questions.a: The Nurse.

weeks.assessment_key: Act 2 quiz answers: 1) Romeo overhears Juliet in the orchard/at the balcony. 2) 'Wherefore art thou Romeo' = why are you Romeo. 3) Juliet asks Romeo to send word about marriage. 4) The Friar was surprised Romeo forgot Rosaline. 5) Friar's reason: end the feud. 6) The Nurse delays giving Juliet the news. 7) They marry in the Friar's cell. Journal: proficient = names a character and supports with two quotations.

weeks.prep: R&J Act 3. Note: Act 3 contains two deaths and Capulet's harsh threats; prepare to discuss.
misconceptions: Blaming Romeo alone for Mercutio's death: Tybalt stabs Mercutio under Romeo's arm as Romeo tries to stop the fight — Mercutio and Tybalt also chose to fight.
Missing the shift in genre: before 3.1 the play has comedy; after, tragedy.
Thinking oxymorons are random: Juliet's oxymorons express her conflict between love for Romeo and grief for Tybalt.

days.guide: Read 3.1; explain how Mercutio's death turns the play to tragedy.

questions.q: Why does Romeo refuse to fight Tybalt at first?
questions.a: He is now secretly married to Juliet, so Tybalt is his kinsman.

questions.q: What does Mercutio's curse 'A plague o' both your houses!' mean?
questions.a: He blames both families' feud for his death; it foreshadows the tragedy.

days.guide: Read 3.2; analyze Juliet's oxymorons.

questions.q: Give two of Juliet's oxymorons about Romeo.
questions.a: 'Beautiful tyrant! fiend angelical! / Dove-feathered raven!' — also 'damnèd saint, an honorable villain.'

days.guide: Read 3.3–3.4; compare Romeo's despair with the Friar's plan.

questions.q: Why does Romeo think banishment is worse than death?
questions.a: Exile from Verona means exile from Juliet — 'heaven is here, where Juliet lives.'

questions.q: What is the Friar's plan in 3.3?
questions.a: Romeo spends the night with Juliet, then goes to Mantua until the marriage can be announced and a pardon obtained.

days.guide: Read 3.5; analyze Capulet's ultimatum and Juliet's isolation.

questions.q: What does Capulet threaten if Juliet won't marry Paris?
questions.a: To disown her — she can 'hang, beg, starve, die in the streets.'

questions.q: How does the Nurse betray Juliet?
questions.a: She advises Juliet to marry Paris and forget Romeo.

days.guide: Act 3 quiz; turning-point paragraph.

questions.q: What does Romeo cry after killing Tybalt?
questions.a: 'O, I am fortune's fool!'

weeks.assessment_key: Act 3 quiz answers: 1) Tybalt kills Mercutio. 2) Romeo kills Tybalt. 3) The Prince banishes Romeo. 4) Juliet's oxymorons show conflicted feelings. 5) Romeo goes to Mantua. 6) Capulet sets the wedding to Paris for Thursday. 7) Lark vs. nightingale = morning has come. 8) The Nurse advises marrying Paris. Turning-point paragraph: Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence.

weeks.prep: R&J Act 4. Parental note: Juliet threatens suicide in 4.1 and drinks a potion she fears may kill her; discuss as a tragic choice, and check in with your teen.
misconceptions: Believing the potion is poison: it causes a deathlike sleep (about 42 hours).
Missing dramatic irony in 4.5: the audience knows Juliet is alive while the family mourns.
Thinking the Friar's plan was 'safe': it depends on a letter reaching Romeo in time.

days.guide: Read 4.1; list the plan's steps and risks.

questions.q: What are the steps of the Friar's plan?
questions.a: Juliet agrees to marry Paris, drinks the potion the night before, appears dead, is placed in the family tomb; the Friar sends a letter to Romeo, who will come to take her to Mantua when she wakes.

questions.q: What could go wrong?
questions.a: The letter might not reach Romeo; she might wake early; the potion might fail.

days.guide: Read the 4.3 soliloquy; annotate her fears.

questions.q: Name three of Juliet's fears.
questions.a: The potion might not work; it might be poison from the Friar; she might wake before Romeo and suffocate or go mad in the tomb among the dead (and Tybalt's corpse).

days.guide: Read 4.4–4.5; chart audience vs. character knowledge.

questions.q: What is ironic in 4.5 when the family finds Juliet?
questions.a: They grieve, believing she is dead, while the audience knows she is only sleeping — and wedding preparations turn to funeral ones.

days.guide: Use context and footnotes for 15 archaic words.

questions.q: Meaning of 'shrift'?
questions.a: Confession (to a priest).

days.guide: Act 4 quiz; prediction letter from Friar John's perspective.

questions.q: Why does Capulet move the wedding up a day?
questions.a: Juliet pretends to agree, and he is so pleased he moves it to Wednesday.

weeks.assessment_key: Act 4 quiz answers: 1) Juliet goes to the Friar's cell (meets Paris there). 2) She threatens to kill herself with a knife. 3) The potion lasts 42 hours. 4) Romeo will learn by letter. 5) The wedding moves to Wednesday. 6) Juliet's soliloquy fears (any two). 7) The Nurse discovers Juliet. Creative letter rubric: accurate to plot, Friar John's voice, explains he hasn't delivered the letter (he will be quarantined).

weeks.prep: R&J Act 5 and a film adaptation (Zeffirelli 1968 is rated PG; Luhrmann 1996 is PG-13 — preview). Parental note: Act 5 contains the double suicide.
misconceptions: Blaming one event alone: the tragedy results from a chain (feud, haste, Tybalt's death, the hurried marriage to Paris, the undelivered letter).
Arguing 'fate' without evidence: use lines such as 'star-crossed' and 'fortune's fool.'
Judging a film as 'better/worse' without analyzing choices (what's added, cut, emphasized).

days.guide: Read 5.1–5.3; your child lists the chain of mistakes.

questions.q: Why doesn't Romeo receive the Friar's letter?
questions.a: Friar John was quarantined because of suspected plague and couldn't deliver it.

questions.q: What news does Balthasar bring Romeo?
questions.a: That Juliet is dead and buried in the Capulet tomb.

days.guide: Your child writes a quick argument about fate vs. choice with three quotations.

questions.q: Quote one line supporting fate.
questions.a: 'A pair of star-crossed lovers' (Prologue) or 'O, I am fortune's fool!' (3.1).

days.guide: Watch the balcony or tomb scene in a film; note additions, cuts, emphases.

questions.q: In Shakespeare's text, why does the Friar leave Juliet in the tomb?
questions.a: He hears the watch coming and fears being caught; Juliet refuses to go.

days.guide: Your child writes a comparison paragraph on page vs. film.

questions.q: What is one choice a director must make that the text leaves open?
questions.a: Setting, costume, which lines to cut, actors' tone and movements, music, camera angles.

days.guide: Act 5 quiz; submit film paragraph.

questions.q: How does the play end?
questions.a: The families reconcile; Montague and Capulet promise gold statues; the Prince: 'For never was a story of more woe / Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.'

weeks.assessment_key: Act 5 quiz answers: 1) Balthasar brings Romeo the news. 2) Romeo buys poison from an apothecary. 3) Friar John's letter was not delivered due to quarantine. 4) Romeo kills Paris at the tomb. 5) Romeo drinks poison. 6) Juliet stabs herself with Romeo's dagger. 7) The feud ends. Film paragraph (RL.9-10.7): 4 = names specific director choices and explains their effect compared with the text; 3 = some comparison; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Full R&J text; simple props. Prepare the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Citing Shakespeare by page: cite act.scene.line, e.g., (3.1.94).
Ignoring counterclaims: acknowledge another character's responsibility.
Memorizing without understanding: paraphrase lines before performing.

days.guide: Your child chooses who bears most responsibility and outlines claim, reasons, counterclaim.

questions.q: Give a reason the Friar bears responsibility.
questions.a: He secretly marries them and devises the risky potion plan, then flees the tomb, leaving Juliet alone.

days.guide: Draft with at least five quotations cited by act, scene, and line.

questions.q: Cite 'These violent delights have violent ends' correctly.
questions.a: (2.6.9) — act 2, scene 6, line 9 (Folger line numbers may vary slightly).

days.guide: Revise counterclaims; edit quotation punctuation (slashes for line breaks).

questions.q: How do you quote two lines of verse within a sentence?
questions.a: Use a slash with spaces: 'It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden, / Too like the lightning' (2.2.125–126; line numbers vary slightly by edition).

days.guide: Memorize 15–20 lines; plan blocking and vocal choices.

questions.q: What is blocking?
questions.a: Planned movement and positions of actors on stage.

days.guide: Performance, essay submission, Unit 6 test.

questions.q: Who says 'A plague o' both your houses!'?
questions.a: Mercutio.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = precise, arguable thesis; logically ordered body paragraphs each with a topic sentence, embedded quotations cited correctly, and commentary that explains significance; effective transitions; conclusion extends the idea; few errors. 3 = clear thesis, adequate evidence and explanation, some summary, minor errors. 2 = vague thesis, evidence thin or poorly explained, organization uneven. 1 = no clear thesis, little evidence, errors interfere. Performance rubric: memorized (few prompts), clear delivery, vocal expression matches meaning, purposeful movement. Unit 6 test sample answers: Prologue info; Queen Mab speaker (Mercutio); 'Wisely and slow' (Friar); Mercutio's curse; Juliet's oxymorons; potion plan; Friar John's quarantine; dramatic irony in 4.5; ending reconciliation.

weeks.prep: Get To Kill a Mockingbird (library). Read the whole novel before starting or stay ahead. Parental note: the novel includes racial slurs, racism, and a rape accusation at its center; discuss why Lee depicts them and how you'll handle slurs when reading aloud. Gather Library of Congress Depression photos and a Scottsboro Boys overview (1931 case of nine Black teenagers falsely accused in Alabama).
misconceptions: Confusing the adult narrator with child Scout: the narrator is adult Jean Louise looking back with understanding the child lacks.
Treating Boo Radley rumors as facts: they are town gossip and children's imagination.
Seeing setting as background only: Maycomb's poverty, racism, and class structure drive the plot.

days.guide: Study photos and the Scottsboro overview; list three facts.

questions.q: What happened in the Scottsboro case?
questions.a: In 1931, nine Black teenagers in Alabama were falsely accused of raping two white women; despite weak evidence, all-white juries convicted them — a case that exposed racial injustice in the South.

days.guide: Read Chapters 1–3; analyze adult vs. child narration.

questions.q: What lesson does Atticus teach Scout in Chapter 3?
questions.a: 'You never really understand a person until you consider things from his point of view… until you climb into his skin and walk around in it.'

questions.q: What happens with Walter Cunningham at lunch?
questions.a: Scout criticizes him for pouring syrup on his food; Calpurnia scolds her that guests must be treated with respect.

days.guide: Read Chapters 4–6; track changing views of Boo.

questions.q: What do the children find in the knot-hole of the tree?
questions.a: Gum, then two Indian-head pennies (more gifts follow later).

questions.q: What happens to Jem's pants?
questions.a: He loses them on the Radley fence; when he returns, they've been mended and folded over the fence.

days.guide: Compare a newspaper account and a documentary clip of Scottsboro; note emphases.
