questions.q: Why might a 1931 Southern newspaper and a modern documentary tell the Scottsboro story differently?
questions.a: Different audiences, purposes, and time periods — the newspaper may reflect contemporary prejudices; the documentary has historical hindsight and testimony.

days.guide: Quiz on Chapters 1–6; setting paragraph.

questions.q: How does Scout describe Maycomb?
questions.a: As 'a tired old town' — hot, slow, and poor during the Depression.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Narrator: Scout (Jean Louise Finch). 2) Dill visits each summer. 3) Boo (Arthur) Radley. 4) Miss Caroline is the new teacher. 5) Atticus's 'climb into his skin' lesson. 6) Gifts in the knot-hole. 7) Jem's pants mended. 8) Miss Maudie is the neighbor who explains Boo's family. Setting paragraph: Paragraph rubric: 4 = arguable claim, two well-chosen quotations embedded and cited, commentary that explains HOW the evidence proves the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thinner commentary; 2 = summary instead of analysis or only one piece of evidence; 1 = off-topic or no evidence.

weeks.prep: TKAM Chapters 7–11. Theme tracker (empathy, courage, justice, innocence).
misconceptions: Thinking the mockingbird quote is only about birds: it's about harming innocents.
Defining courage as 'a man with a gun': Atticus explicitly rejects that definition.
Seeing Mrs. Dubose as simply mean: her fight against morphine addiction is Atticus's example of real courage.

days.guide: Read Chapters 7–8; analyze the gifts and the fire.

questions.q: What gifts appear in the tree in Chapter 7?
questions.a: Soap figures carved to look like Jem and Scout, a pocket watch and chain, a spelling medal, and gum.

questions.q: What happens during the fire at Miss Maudie's?
questions.a: Someone puts a blanket around Scout's shoulders without her noticing — it was Boo Radley.

days.guide: Read Chapter 9; explain why Atticus defends Tom.

questions.q: Why does Atticus take Tom Robinson's case?
questions.a: Because it's right; if he didn't, he 'couldn't hold up my head in town' or tell his children what to do.

questions.q: What does Atticus say about trying even when you will lose?
questions.a: 'Simply because we were licked a hundred years before we started is no reason for us not to try to win.'

days.guide: Read Chapter 10; explain the mockingbird quote.

questions.q: Why is it 'a sin to kill a mockingbird'?
questions.a: Miss Maudie explains that mockingbirds only make music for us; they do no harm — so harming them (innocents) is wrong.

questions.q: What does the mad-dog scene reveal about Atticus?
questions.a: He's an excellent shot ('One-Shot Finch') but doesn't boast — showing humility and restraint.

days.guide: Read Chapter 11; write about Atticus's definition of courage.

questions.q: How does Atticus define real courage?
questions.a: 'It's when you know you're licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what.'

days.guide: Quiz on Chapters 7–11; update theme tracker with six quotations.

questions.q: What did Mrs. Dubose struggle against before she died?
questions.a: Morphine addiction — she was determined to die free of it.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: 1) Nathan Radley fills the knot-hole with cement. 2) Boo puts the blanket on Scout. 3) Atticus defends Tom Robinson. 4) Mockingbirds harm no one. 5) Atticus shoots the mad dog (Tim Johnson). 6) Jem destroys Mrs. Dubose's camellias. 7) His punishment: reading to her. 8) She was overcoming morphine addiction. Theme tracker: proficient = six accurate quotes with page numbers and theme connections.

weeks.prep: TKAM Chapters 12–19. Evidence chart for the trial (witness, claim, evidence against). Preview Chapters 17–19 for mature trial content.
misconceptions: Thinking the trial evidence is ambiguous: the text shows Mayella's injuries were on her right side, likely from a left-handed attacker; Bob Ewell is left-handed and Tom's left arm is crippled.
Missing why Tom's 'I felt sorry for her' hurts him: in 1930s Maycomb, a Black man pitying a white woman was seen as overstepping.
Seeing the mob scene as luck: Scout's innocent talk reminds Mr. Cunningham of his humanity — empathy works.

days.guide: Read Chapters 12–13; compare Calpurnia's two worlds and Aunt Alexandra.

questions.q: Why does Calpurnia speak differently at First Purchase church?
questions.a: She talks like her community there; she says it's not necessary to show off to people who would think she was 'puttin' on airs.'

questions.q: What are Aunt Alexandra's ideas of family?
questions.a: She stresses 'fine folks' and family heritage/background, judging people by lineage.

days.guide: Read Chapters 14–15; analyze how Scout disperses the mob.

questions.q: How does Scout break up the mob at the jail?
questions.a: She innocently talks to Mr. Cunningham about his entailment and his son Walter, making him see the situation as a father and neighbor; he tells the men to leave.

days.guide: Read Chapters 16–18; record witness claims and contradicting evidence.

questions.q: What does Atticus establish about Bob Ewell's handedness and why does it matter?
questions.a: Ewell is left-handed; Mayella's injuries were mostly on the right side of her face, consistent with a left-handed attacker.

questions.q: What important fact about medical care comes out?
questions.a: No one called a doctor for Mayella.

days.guide: Read Chapter 19; analyze 'I felt sorry for her.'

questions.q: Why can't Tom have hit Mayella as described?
questions.a: His left arm was crippled in a cotton gin accident; he couldn't have choked and beaten her the way she claimed.

questions.q: Why does Tom's statement 'I felt right sorry for her' damage him with the jury?
questions.a: The white jury sees a Black man pitying a white woman as insulting his 'place' in the social order.

days.guide: Your child writes a mock closing argument for the defense.

questions.q: What is the strongest physical evidence for the defense?
questions.a: Tom's useless left arm versus injuries on the right side of Mayella's face, plus no doctor called.

weeks.assessment_key: Mock closing rubric: 4 = cites at least three pieces of trial evidence (left-handedness, right-side injuries, Tom's arm, no doctor, inconsistencies in testimony), addresses the jury persuasively with appeals, logically organized; 3 = two pieces of evidence; 2 = mostly emotional; 1 = inaccurate. Evidence chart: Heck Tate — right eye injury, no doctor; Bob Ewell — left-handed; Mayella — inconsistent, avoids questions; Tom — crippled left arm, helped Mayella with chores.

weeks.prep: TKAM Chapters 20–26. Seminar rubric. Note: Tom's death (Chapter 24) is upsetting; discuss.
misconceptions: Thinking the verdict shows Atticus failed: Miss Maudie notes the jury deliberated for hours — 'a baby step' toward justice.
Missing hypocrisy in Chapter 26: Miss Gates condemns Hitler's persecution yet expressed racist views after the trial.
Believing Atticus's rhetoric is only emotional: his closing uses logos (evidence), ethos, and pathos.

days.guide: Read Chapters 20–21; analyze appeals in Atticus's closing.

questions.q: Give an example of logos and pathos in Atticus's closing.
questions.a: Logos: no medical evidence and evidence the attacker was left-handed. Pathos: 'In the name of God, do your duty' / appeal to the courts as 'the great levelers.'

questions.q: How do the people in the balcony honor Atticus after the verdict?
questions.a: They stand as he passes — 'Miss Jean Louise, stand up. Your father's passin'.'

days.guide: Read Chapters 22–23; compare reactions.

questions.q: How does Miss Maudie comfort Jem?
questions.a: She says some men are 'born to do our unpleasant jobs for us' and that the long deliberation was progress.

questions.q: How does Atticus respond when Bob Ewell spits on him?
questions.a: He wipes his face and walks away, saying he'd rather Ewell take it out on him than on his children.

days.guide: Read Chapters 24–25; analyze Underwood's editorial.

questions.q: How does Tom die?
questions.a: He is shot (seventeen times) while trying to escape from prison.

questions.q: What does Mr. Underwood compare Tom's death to?
questions.a: 'The senseless slaughter of songbirds by hunters and children' — connecting Tom to the mockingbird symbol.

days.guide: Read Chapter 26; identify Miss Gates's hypocrisy.

questions.q: What is Miss Gates's hypocrisy?
questions.a: She condemns Hitler's persecution of the Jews, but Scout heard her say after the trial that Black people needed to be 'taught a lesson.'

days.guide: Seminar on justice in Maycomb; quiz.

questions.q: What is the verdict?
questions.a: Guilty.

weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric: 4 = uses quotations from the trial and aftermath, considers multiple characters' views, builds on others; 3 = some evidence; 2 = opinions only; 1 = minimal. Quiz answers: 1) Verdict: guilty. 2) Reverend Sykes tells Scout to stand. 3) Jem cries. 4) Bob Ewell spits on Atticus. 5) Tom is shot escaping. 6) Underwood compares it to killing songbirds. 7) Miss Gates teaches about Hitler/democracy. 8) Her hypocrisy.

weeks.prep: TKAM Chapters 27–31. Essay planner. Prepare the Unit 7 test. Note: Chapter 28 includes an attack on the children.
misconceptions: Assuming Jem killed Bob Ewell: Boo Radley killed him while defending the children; Heck Tate reports Ewell 'fell on his knife.'
Missing the structure: the novel ends where it began — with Boo — completing Scout's growth in empathy.
Thinking Heck Tate's decision is simply lying: he protects a shy, innocent man — 'a sin' like killing a mockingbird.

days.guide: Read Chapters 27–28; analyze suspense in the attack.

questions.q: How does Lee build suspense on Halloween?
questions.a: Darkness, Scout's limited view from inside the ham costume, strange sounds of someone following, and the shortcut through the dark.

days.guide: Read Chapters 29–31; explain the porch scene.

questions.q: What does Scout say when she recognizes Boo?
questions.a: 'Hey, Boo.'

questions.q: How does standing on the Radley porch complete the empathy theme?
questions.a: Scout sees the neighborhood from Boo's point of view — 'Atticus was right… you never really know a man until you stand in his shoes and walk around in them.'

days.guide: Plan a theme essay (empathy, courage, or justice).

questions.q: Give three moments that trace the empathy theme.
questions.a: Atticus's 'climb into his skin' lesson (Ch. 3), Scout talking down the mob (Ch. 15), standing on Boo's porch (Ch. 31).

days.guide: Draft and revise the 900-word essay with at least six quotations.

questions.q: Why does Scout agree with Heck Tate's decision?
questions.a: She says exposing Boo would be 'sort of like shootin' a mockingbird.'

days.guide: Submit essay; Unit 7 test.

questions.q: Who carries Jem home after the attack?
questions.a: Boo Radley.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric (4 levels): 4 = precise, arguable thesis; logically ordered body paragraphs each with a topic sentence, embedded quotations cited correctly, and commentary that explains significance; effective transitions; conclusion extends the idea; few errors. 3 = clear thesis, adequate evidence and explanation, some summary, minor errors. 2 = vague thesis, evidence thin or poorly explained, organization uneven. 1 = no clear thesis, little evidence, errors interfere. Unit 7 test sample answers: narrator perspective; Scottsboro connection; knot-hole gifts; Atticus's definition of courage; mockingbird meaning; Scout and the mob; Tom's arm and the left-handed evidence; verdict; Underwood's editorial; Miss Gates; Boo saves the children; 'Hey, Boo'; porch scene.

weeks.prep: Library card and database access (e.g., Gale or EBSCO via your public library). Purdue OWL annotated bibliography page. A lateral-reading checklist (who is behind this source? what do other sites say about it?).
misconceptions: Choosing questions that are too broad ('the Greeks') or answerable with one fact.
Judging credibility by how a site looks or its .org domain: read laterally — leave the site and see what others say about it.
Annotations that only summarize: also evaluate credibility and usefulness.

days.guide: Brainstorm topics from the year's texts; narrow to one researchable question.

questions.q: Narrow 'juvenile justice' into a researchable question.
questions.a: Sample: 'Do diversion programs reduce repeat offenses among teens compared with juvenile detention?'

days.guide: Teach lateral reading; your child evaluates five websites with the checklist.

questions.q: What is lateral reading?
questions.a: Opening new tabs to research the source itself — who publishes it, their funding and reputation — instead of judging only from the site.

days.guide: Locate six sources (two print/database); write three annotated entries.

questions.q: What does an annotated bibliography entry include?
questions.a: The MLA citation, a summary of the source's main points, and an evaluation of its credibility and usefulness.

days.guide: Write objective summaries of two key sources.

questions.q: What should an objective summary avoid?
questions.a: Personal opinion and minor details; it states the central idea and key supporting points.

days.guide: Submit question and bibliography for approval.

questions.q: Why include print or database sources?
questions.a: They are usually edited/peer-reviewed and give more reliable, deeper information.

weeks.assessment_key: Annotated bibliography rubric: 4 = six credible, relevant sources in correct MLA format with annotations summarizing and evaluating each; 3 = minor formatting errors or thin evaluations; 2 = fewer than six or weak sources; 1 = incomplete. Approved question: focused, debatable or explorable, researchable with available sources.

weeks.prep: Annotated bibliography; note cards or a digital notes document labeled by source and topic.
misconceptions: Paraphrasing by swapping a few words: a paraphrase restates the idea in your own structure and words and still needs a citation.
Outlining source-by-source: group evidence by idea so sources 'talk to each other' (synthesis).
Dropping quotes without signal phrases ('According to …').

days.guide: Practice paraphrasing vs. quoting with 6 passages.

questions.q: When should you quote rather than paraphrase?
questions.a: When the exact wording is powerful, precise, or authoritative; otherwise paraphrase.

days.guide: Build an outline grouping evidence by idea.

questions.q: What does 'synthesis' mean in research writing?
questions.a: Combining information from several sources to support one point, showing how they relate.

days.guide: Draft the introduction and first half with signal phrases.

questions.q: Give an example of a signal phrase.
questions.a: 'According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, …' or 'Historian X argues that…'

days.guide: Finish the draft with a conclusion that answers the research question.

questions.q: What should the conclusion of a research paper do?
questions.a: Answer the research question, summarize key findings, and note significance or remaining questions.

days.guide: Format the MLA Works Cited page; submit the full draft.

questions.q: How is a Works Cited page ordered?
questions.a: Alphabetically by the first word of each entry (usually the author's last name), with hanging indents and double spacing.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft rubric: 4 = 1,200–1,500 words, clear thesis answering the question, evidence synthesized from multiple sources, signal phrases and in-text citations, conclusion answers the question, correct MLA Works Cited; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = source-by-source summary, citation problems; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Research draft; slide software; a revision checklist (thesis, synthesis, transitions, citations, MLA format).
misconceptions: Revision = proofreading: revise ideas, structure, and evidence first; edit sentences last.
Slides crowded with text: use images, a chart, and key words; say the details aloud.
Colon after a verb or semicolon before a list (see Weeks 5–6).

days.guide: Conference on the draft; your child revises for synthesis and transitions.

questions.q: Name two transitions that show contrast.
questions.a: However, on the other hand (also nevertheless, in contrast).

days.guide: Edit for MLA format, parallel structure, and semicolons/colons.

questions.q: Correct: 'The study found three causes; poor sleep, stress, and diet.'
questions.a: Use a colon: 'The study found three causes: poor sleep, stress, and diet.'

days.guide: Build a 6–8 slide presentation with images, a chart, and minimal text.

questions.q: What is a good rule for text on slides?
questions.a: A few key words or a short phrase per point — the speaker explains the rest.

days.guide: Write speaker notes; rehearse a 6-minute talk.

questions.q: What should speaker notes contain?
questions.a: Key points, transitions, and data to mention — not a full script to read word for word.

days.guide: Submit the final paper and a reflection on revision choices.

questions.q: What is one thing a revision reflection should explain?
questions.a: A specific change made and why it improved the paper.

weeks.assessment_key: Final research paper rubric (W.9-10.7): 4 = focused question answered with a clear thesis; synthesis of 6+ credible sources; accurate paraphrase/quotation with MLA citations; logical organization and transitions; correct Works Cited; few errors. 3 = adequate with minor issues; 2 = summary-heavy, weak citation; 1 = incomplete or plagiarized content (rewrite required).

weeks.prep: Presentation slides; portfolio folder (narrative, literary analysis, argument, research). Choose a TED-Ed talk for evaluation. Prepare the final exam (unseen literary and informational passages plus a timed argument essay).
misconceptions: Reading slides aloud: look at the audience and speak from notes.
Portfolio reflections that only praise: name specific growth with evidence and a goal.
Arguing in a timed essay without a counterclaim.

days.guide: Your child presents to family or a co-op and answers questions.

questions.q: What should you do if you don't know the answer to an audience question?
questions.a: Admit it honestly, offer what you do know, and say how you would find out.

days.guide: Your child evaluates another speaker with a rubric.

questions.q: What makes a speaker's reasoning strong?
questions.a: Clear claims supported by relevant, credible evidence and logical connections; no fallacies.

days.guide: Assemble the portfolio of best work.

questions.q: Why include drafts as well as finals?
questions.a: They show growth and revision choices.

days.guide: Write the reflection letter on growth and goals.

questions.q: What should the reflection letter include?
questions.a: Specific strengths and growth with examples from the portfolio, a challenge overcome, and goals for English 10.

days.guide: Final exam.

questions.q: What are the parts of a strong argument essay?
questions.a: Precise claim, reasons with evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal, conclusion.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = clear organization, eye contact, appropriate pace, visuals that support, handles questions, within time; 3 = minor issues; 2 = reads from slides; 1 = incomplete. Reflection letter: 4 = specific evidence of growth across genres and concrete goals. Final exam: reading items 80%+ proficient; timed argument essay scored with the W.9-10.1 argument rubric (Week 12).
